1.pericope_label: Nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations
debates: Whether the verse threatens a worse affliction or promises a lighter one
Where the division between the chapters should fall
Why these two tribes are named rather than the whole land
outliers: Ellicott calls the received version almost unintelligible and replaces it wholesale, turning the second half from a record of affliction into a promise of honour
Gill takes the oppressor for a Roman general and the affliction for the siege of Jerusalem, where the rest read an Assyrian invasion
themes: A word that turns a sentence around
Two border tribes taking the first blow
A light judgment tried before a heavy one
Bounds set to the darkness itself

2.pericope_label: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined. Thou hast multiplied the nation, and not increased the joy: they joy before thee according to the joy in harvest, and as men rejoice when they divide the spoil
debates: Who the people walking in darkness are
Whether the joy was increased or withheld
How far the Gospel use of the words matches what the prophet meant
outliers: Ellicott holds that the Evangelist gave the words a further meaning than the prophet had in mind, where Calvin argues the two meanings are one
Calvin lists five current explanations of the difficult clause and rejects every one before offering his own
themes: A light seen by people still walking in the dark
One letter that decides whether a verse is glad or grim
Harvest joy and the joy of dividing spoil
A small remnant called a multiplied nation

4.pericope_label: For thou hast broken the yoke of his burden, and the staff of his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, as in the day of Midian. For every battle of the warrior is with confused noise, and garments rolled in blood; but this shall be with burning and fuel of fire
debates: What yoke is broken
What the word found only here means
Whether the burning consumes the enemy or the weapons
outliers: Clarke supports his rendering from a Roman coin and a line of Virgil, taking the burning of captured armour for a standing emblem of peace
Gill reads the broken yoke wholly of the ceremonial law, of Satan and of sin, where the others keep an oppressor of flesh and blood in view
themes: A rod that drove men to their labour
Three hundred men remembered for centuries
A boot that made the ground ring
Armour heaped up and set alight

6.pericope_label: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace
debates: Whether the child is a king of Judah or the Messiah
Whether the titles are one name or several
What is meant by the government resting on a shoulder
outliers: Clarke reports a thirteenth-century manuscript that inserts a clause about a stumbling-block, a reading he says is nowhere else acknowledged
Ellicott derives the very form of the name from the long epithet-lists that the kings of Egypt and Assyria gave themselves
themes: A child spoken of as already reigning
An ensign of office carried on the shoulder
Eight words that make a single name
A short freedom that was never the point

7.pericope_label: Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will perform this
debates: What the irregular letter in the first word signifies
Whether the perpetuity belongs to a dynasty or to one person
How a kingdom already everlasting can be said to increase
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch report a rabbinic tradition that the letter was closed because a king of Judah was found unworthy to be the Messiah
Ellicott prefers a personal immortality of sovereignty over the perpetuity of a royal line, against the parallels usually cited
themes: A letter shut where it should be open
A kingdom that looks about to perish and does not
A seed that becomes a tree full of nests
Love spoken of as jealousy

8.pericope_label: The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it hath lighted upon Israel
debates: Whether the threat falls on the northern kingdom only or on all Israel
Whether the two names stand for one people or two
What kind of word was sent
outliers: Ellicott takes both names for the kingdom of Judah, holding the northern kingdom no longer worthy of the name of Israel
Keil and Delitzsch reject the majority reading that confines the section to Ephraim, and deny that the scourging had already happened when the words were spoken
themes: A word sent ahead of the blow
Two names for one doomed people
Threats turned into jest as if breath could stop a storm
Hail falling on men who would not listen

9.pericope_label: And all the people shall know, even Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria, that say in the pride and stoutness of heart, The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones: the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars
debates: What the verb shall know governs
Whether the ruin boasted over is literal
What the boast reveals about the speakers
outliers: Clarke treats the missing object as a corruption and adopts an ancient version that makes the verb mean carrying themselves haughtily
Calvin turns the boast on his own continent, where he says decades of chastisement have only increased luxury
themes: A sentence with its object missing
Mud walls answered by cut stone
Coarse timber traded for cedar in a boast
Losses counted as an opportunity to build better

11.pericope_label: Therefore the Lord shall set up the adversaries of Rezin against him, and join his enemies together; The Syrians before, and the Philistines behind; and they shall devour Israel with open mouth. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still
debates: Who the adversaries set up are
Whether before and behind mean east and west
What the closing refrain marks
outliers: Clarke reports two variant readings, one making the adversaries the princes of the fallen ally and one substituting Mount Zion for the name of the king
Calvin rejects the compass reading the others adopt, taking the words for an attack from every side at once
themes: An ally whose fall leaves a flank open
A letter scraped out and written over
Friends who change sides in a moment
Scourges kept back and paid out by degrees

13.pericope_label: For the people turneth not unto him that smiteth them, neither do they seek the Lord of hosts. Therefore the Lord will cut off from Israel head and tail, branch and rush, in one day. The ancient and honourable, he is the head; and the prophet that teacheth lies, he is the tail
debates: Why repeated blows produced no repentance
Who the head and the tail stand for
Whether the explanatory verse belongs to the text
outliers: Ellicott reports that some critics strike the explanatory verse out as a marginal note that crept into the text, and defends it
Calvin denies that calling the false prophets the tail is a term of contempt, taking it only for the lowest part of one body
themes: A rod that corrects nobody
Palm branch and bulrush cut on the same day
Guilt hidden behind the number of the guilty
Guides more contemptible than those they mislead

16.pericope_label: For the leaders of this people cause them to err; and they that are led of them are destroyed. Therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men, neither shall have mercy on their fatherless and widows: for every one is an hypocrite and an evildoer. For wickedness burneth as the fire: it shall devour the briers and thorns
debates: What the leaders did or failed to do
Why the young and the bereaved are not spared
Whether the fire is the sin or the punishment
outliers: Calvin refuses to let bad rulers excuse those they misled, holding that none are ruined by treacherous guides but those willing to be led astray
Ellicott alone finds a clearing in the burning, with the land left ready for fresh culture and a better growth
themes: Guides who let their charges do as they please
Widows and orphans passed over by mercy
Sins that fan the fire that consumes them
A thicket that catches and spreads flame

19.pericope_label: Through the wrath of the Lord of hosts is the land darkened, and the people shall be as the fuel of the fire: no man shall spare his brother. And he shall snatch on the right hand, and be hungry; and he shall eat on the left hand, and they shall not be satisfied: they shall eat every man the flesh of his own arm: Manasseh, Ephraim; and Ephraim, Manasseh: and they together shall be against Judah
debates: Whether the land is darkened or burned
Whether the flesh eaten is a man own arm or his neighbour
Why two closely related tribes turn on each other
outliers: Clarke emends the text so that men devour the flesh of their neighbour rather than their own arm, and argues the next verse proves it
Gill reports a rendering in which the land is burned rather than darkened, resting the received sense on a word found nowhere else
themes: Smoke thick enough to put out the light
A nation left with no enemy but itself
Beasts that will not eat their own kind
Blows that do not stop while the struck refuse to turn
